nameStory: Rough cottongrass gets its name from the fluffy, cotton-like white tufts that crown each seed head in late summer. The 'rough' part refers to the texture of its narrow leaves, which feel slightly sandpapery when you run your fingers along them. Despite its name, it's not actually a grass at all, but a member of the sedge family!
description: Rough cottongrass is a delicate wetland sedge that grows in small clumps, typically reaching 8-16 inches tall. In summer, it produces distinctive fluffy white seed heads that look like tiny cotton balls dancing on slender stems. The plant has narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the base, and thin triangular stems that are characteristic of sedges. It's one of the smaller and more graceful members of the cottongrass family.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Fluffy white cotton-like tufts appear in late summer, each about the size of a marble, nodding gracefully on thin stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves feel slightly rough or sandpapery to the touch when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, triangular stems that you can feel have three distinct sides when rolled between your thumb and finger

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, delicate clumps rather than large tussocks, staying relatively short at under 2 feet tall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny brownish flowers appear in small clusters before transforming into the signature cotton-ball seed heads

habitat: Rough cottongrass thrives in acidic bogs, wet meadows, and the soggy margins of ponds and slow streams throughout New England. You'll find it in areas with consistently moist, peaty soils, often growing alongside sphagnum moss, cranberries, and other bog plants. It prefers open, sunny wetlands rather than shaded swamps.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from soggy ground, with narrow leaves growing in small tufts. The plant is inconspicuous but identifiable by its triangular stems and rough-textured leaves.
seasonality.summer: Small brownish flower clusters appear in early summer, followed by the development of the characteristic white cotton-ball seed heads by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: The fluffy white seed heads persist and become even more prominent as surrounding vegetation dies back, creating a striking contrast against autumn colors.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and old seed head remnants may persist above snow, appearing as small brown stalks in frozen wetlands.

funFact: Those fluffy white 'cotton balls' are actually thousands of silky bristles attached to tiny seeds - each bristle acts like a parachute, allowing the seeds to float on the wind for miles to find new boggy homes!
confusionNotes: Rough cottongrass is easily confused with its larger cousin, tawny cottongrass, but rough cottongrass is much smaller and more delicate overall. Remember: rough cottongrass stays low and dainty, while tawny cottongrass grows tall and robust in bigger clumps.
contextualKnowledge: Like all cottongrasses, this plant is actually a sedge, not a true grass. The common name can be misleading - remember the old botanist's rhyme: 'sedges have edges' (triangular stems), while grasses have round, hollow stems. This helps avoid confusion when learning plant families.
compareHints: Rough cottongrass is the smallest and most delicate of New England's cottongrasses. While tawny cottongrass forms large tussocks and can reach 4 feet tall, rough cottongrass stays petite at under 2 feet. Common cottongrass has multiple cotton-ball heads per stem, while rough cottongrass typically has just one fluffy head per slender stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cottongrasses, tawny cottongrass is unique for its brown seed heads - common cottongrass and tussock cottongrass both have white or cream-colored fluff.
Tussock cottongrass is the only cottongrass that grows in distinctive single tussocks and produces just one seed head per stem.
Among New England's cottongrasses, green-keeled stands out with its bright white seed heads and prominently ridged leaves.
Common cottongrass typically has multiple nodding seed heads per stem, while tussock cottongrass usually has just one erect cottony head per stem.
Among New England's cottongrasses, slender cottongrass stands out for its thin, delicate build and preference for the wettest bog conditions.
